questions_and_answers.question: What is 'moshi moshi' used like in a Japanese telephone conversation?

answers.answer: Like 'hello' — to begin a conversation or when you have a bad connection

questions_and_answers.question: In some homes, the person may say the name first without 'moshi moshi'. What do they say?
How do you make sure you are calling the right place?

answers.answer: (name)-san no otaku desu ka? (Is this (name)'s residence?)

questions_and_answers.question: If it's the right place, how will the person who answers probably respond?

answers.answer: Hai, soo desu. / Hai, sayoo de gozaimasu. (Yes, it is.)

questions_and_answers.question: What is 'Sayoo de gozaimasu' in relation to 'Soo desu'?

answers.answer: A more polite equivalent of 'Soo desu'

questions_and_answers.question: Why do people tend to use especially polite and humble expressions in telephone conversation?

answers.answer: In a conversation that is not face-to-face, there is no way to show politeness except through very polite language
Because it is required by law
Because bowing works over the phone

questions_and_answers.question: If you reach a wrong number, what will the person who answers probably say?
How do you apologize for a wrong number, and how does the person reply?

answers.answer: Doomo sumimasen. -> Iie (doo itashimashite). (I'm sorry. -> No, not at all.)
Shitsuree desu ga. -> Hai, soo desu.

questions_and_answers.question: After confirming the right place, how do you ask for the person you want to talk to?
How can you refer to Mr. Tanaka (someone else's husband) and to Mrs. Tanaka when asking for them?

answers.answer: Use 'goshujin' for the husband and 'okusan' for the wife, no matter who answers

questions_and_answers.question: If the person who answers is the one you want, what will s/he probably say?
When the person leaves the phone to get the one you want, what will s/he probably say?

answers.answer: Chotto matte kudasai. / Shooshoo omachi kudasai. (Please wait a moment.)

questions_and_answers.question: When you ask for the person you want, why is it appropriate to identify yourself by name and company affiliation?

answers.answer: This way you also avoid being asked who you are
It is required to make a call
It is considered rude not to shout

questions_and_answers.question: Which expression means 'I'm (your name) from the American Embassy. May I talk to your husband?'

answers.answer: Amerika Taishikan no (your name) desu ga, goshujin irasshaimasu ka?
Amerika Taishikan wa doko desu ka?
Goshujin wa Amerika Taishikan desu ka?

articles.text:
1. How to get the person you want to talk to

In this lesson, you will learn expressions to use when you place or answer a telephone call at home.

Moshi moshi is used exactly like 'hello' in an English telephone conversation—you can use it when you begin a conversation or you can use it when you have a bad connection. Thus, in most cases the person who answers will first say moshi moshi. However, in some homes, the person may say the name first without moshi moshi. In that case, the person will say:

(name) de gozaimasu.    This is (name)'s residence.

After getting an answer, you usually make sure that you are calling the right place (except when the person says his/her name first). You can do this by asking:

(name)-san no otaku desu ka?    Is this (name)'s residence?

If it's the right place, the person who answers will probably say the following:

Hai, soo desu.
or
Hai, sayoo de gozaimasu.    Yes, it is.

Sayoo de gozaimasu is a more polite equivalent of Soo desu. Ordinarily, people tend to use especially polite and humble expressions in telephone conversation. One reason for this is that in a conversation that is not face-to-face, there is no way to show politeness except through very polite language. Bowing, for example, will not do any good.

If you reach a wrong number, the person who answers will probably say:

(Iie), chigaimasu (yo).    No, it isn't.

Then apologize for the wrong number. You can use the following familiar expression:

Doomo sumimasen.    I'm sorry.

Then the person will probably reply by saying the following:

Iie (doo itashimashite).    No, (not at all).

After confirming that the place you are calling is the right one, you ask for the person you want to talk to. For this purpose, you can use the following expression:

(name)-san irasshaimasu ka?    Is (name) in/at home?

If you want to talk to Mr. Tanaka, for example, you can say either:

Tanaka-san irasshaimasu ka?
OR
Goshujin irasshaimasu ka?

As you learned in Lesson 5, goshujin refers to someone else's husband. However, the word literally means 'master/head (of the house)'. Thus, even if the person who answers is not the wife, you can still use the word goshujin in the above situation. The same thing applies when you are calling Mrs. Tanaka. You can use the word okusan no matter who answers the telephone.

If the person who answers the telephone is the one you want, s/he will probably say:

Wata(ku)shi desu (ga).    Speaking. (literally, 'It's me, but... [what do you want?]')

When the person who answers leaves the phone to get the person you want, s/he will probably say the following:

Chotto matte kudasai.
OR
Shooshoo omachi kudasai.    Please wait a moment.

Shooshoo is politer than chotto (both mean 'a little bit'), and omachi kudasai is politer than matte kudasai.

When you ask for the person you want, it is appropriate to identify yourself both by name and company affiliation. (This way you also avoid being asked who you are.) You can use the following expression for this purpose:

(work place) no (name) desu.    I'm (name) of (work place).

Thus, if you want to talk to Mr. Tanaka, you will say something like the following:

Amerika Taishikan no (your name) desu ga, goshujin irasshaimasu ka?    I'm (your name) from the American Embassy. May I talk to Mr. Tanaka/your husband, etc.?
